Anatomy
Long bone growth/fracture healing is endochondral.
Vessel invades cartilage in the primary ossification center, and growth occurs longitudinally
at either end as chondrocytes proliferate, hypertrophy, die, and are replaced by calcified
matrix and osteoblasts.
Widening of the bone is achieved by osteoblasts differentiating from stem cells from the
ring of LaCroix/nodes of Ranvier.
Flat bone growth/distraction osteogenesis is intramembranous.
The skull is formed by neural crest cells invading a connective tissue scaffold.
The clavicle has intramembranous and endochondral ossification.
The scapula has seven ossification centers.
Physiology
An endochondral epiphyseal plate is divided into four main zones.
The reserve zone has no associated diseases.
Achondroplasia affects the proliferative zone.
Fractures occur in the hypertrophic zone.
In the zone of calcification, type X collagen is present, but type II collagen is predominant.
Calcifying fracture callus has some type IV collagen.

The most common skeletal dysplasia
Autosomal dominant but 80% are new mutations


Achondroplasia
Based on membership in the Little People of America, achondroplasia is the most
common form of dwarfism in the United States and the world. It is inherited in an
autosomal dominant manner; however, approximately 80% of cases are new mutations.
Patients have rhizomelic dwarfism with a relatively preserved spinal height. Substantial
frontal bossing with a flat midface is present.
Pseudoachondroplasia (Table 1)
Short-limbed rhizomelic dwarfism with normal facial features
Normal development before age 2 years

Pseudoachondroplasia

Although pseudoachondroplasia is a rarer form of dwarfism compared with
achondroplasia, patients with pseudoachondroplasia have more disability, particularly
related to joint pain. Facial features tend to be more normal appearing, and
development is normal before age 2 years.
Diastrophic dysplasia (Table 1)
Short-limbed dwarfism apparent from birth with other common findings, including cleft palate
and hitchhiker thumbs (Figures 1 and 2).

Diastrophic dysplasia
Diastrophic dysplasia is an autosomal recessive form of dwarfism characterized by
hitchhiker thumbs. In addition, some patients have cleft palates. Many patients have
substantial disability from joint abnormalities.
Cleidocranial dysostosis (Table 1)
Proportionate dwarfism characterized by mild short stature, a broad forehead, and absent
clavicles.

Cleidocranial dysostosis
Cleidocranial dysostosis is a disorder characterized by mild short stature and partial or
completely missing clavicle bones in some patients. Because the genetic defect affects
osteoblast development, low bone density and fractures are not uncommon.
Mucopolysaccharidoses disorders (Table 2)
A group of lysosomal storage diseases that result in the intracellular accumulation of
mucopolysaccharides in multiple organs. All patients are short statured; additional features
vary but often include corneal clouding, enlarged skulls, bullet-shaped phalanges, intellectual
disability, visceromegaly, cervical instability (C1-C2), genu valgum, and late onset hip dysplasia.

Management
Hurler syndrome can be managed via bone marrow transplantation in the first year of life, but
enzyme replacement therapy also is available; intelligence is normal in some affected
individuals, but short stature and orthopaedic deformities always are present.
Surgical management is indicated for cervical instability (frequently atlantoaxial; dynamic
flexion/extension radiographs and MRI are used) and progressive lower extremity deformity
(Figure 3).
Peripheral nerve compression, such as carpal tunnel syndrome, is common and often requires
surgical decompression.
Enzyme replacement therapies are available for several types, such as Morquio syndrome
(mucopolysaccharidoses type IV).

Mucopolysaccharidoses disorders
The mucopolysaccharidoses are a group of lysosomal storage diseases characterized by
the buildup of mucopolysaccharides in various organs, bones, and joints. Many of these
disorders can be managed via enzyme replacement therapy; therefore, making a
diagnosis as early as possible is beneficial. Although the classic phenotype for these
patients involves short stature, visceromegaly, scoliosis, and coarse features, some
patients do not have all these features early in life or may have milder mutations that do
not present typically. Therefore, these diagnoses should be considered in patients with
typical bone phenotypes.
Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia (MED) (Table 1)
Multiple epiphyseal involvement but no spinal involvement. Often diagnosed in school-aged
children with normal height early. In adulthood, children typically are short for their families
but not short for the general population.


Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia
Patients with MED typically present with radiographic changes of multiple epiphyses with
large joint (hip and knee) pain during middle childhood with exercise. The spine is not
affected. Children typically are short for their families, but they are not short for the
general population (ie, they do not have dwarfism).
Spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia (SED) (Table 1)
Proportionate dwarfism with spinal involvement and a barrel chest. Extremely short stature.

Spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia
Patients with SED have symptoms similar to those with MED but also have spine
involvement, typically platyspondyly, associated with short stature. Many different genes
are causative.
Etiology
Achondroplasia
Mutation affects a single protein in fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3), changing
glycine to arginine at position 380.
Result is growth retardation of the proliferative zone of the epiphyseal plate, resulting in short
limbs.
The growth plates with the most growth (proximal humerus/distal femur) are most affected,
resulting in rhizomelic (proximal more than distal) short stature.

Achondroplasia

Most patients with achondroplasia (98%) have a single mutation in the FGFR3. The
remainder of patients have two other mutations. Therefore, genetic testing for
achondroplasia always is diagnostic. The mutation stops growth of cartilage in the
growth plate, resulting in shorter bones. Patients have rhizomelic shortening, meaning
the limbs are shorter proximally more than distally. The spine is relatively spared.
Current therapies targeting the growth plate to prevent this growth retardation are
being investigated in clinical trials.
Pseudoachondroplasia (Table 1)
Autosomal dominant
Mutation is in cartilage oligomeric matrix protein on chromosome 19.
Epiphyses are delayed and abnormal, metaphyseal flaring is present, and early-onset
osteoarthritis is common.

Pseudoachondroplasia
Pseudoachondroplasia is caused by mutations in cartilage oligomeric matrix protein.
Radiographs demonstrate abnormal-appearing epiphyses and metaphyseal flaring.
Patients have early onset osteoarthritis, and pain may be quite debilitating for some
patients.
Diastrophic dysplasia (Table 1)
Autosomal recessive
Mutation in sulfate transport protein that primarily affects cartilage matrix. Present in 1 in 70
Finnish citizens.

Diastrophic dysplasia

Diastrophic dysplasia is an autosomal recessive disorder. It is caused by a mutation in a
sulfate transport protein that affects cartilage matrix. This issue with cartilage matrix
likely explains increased joint problems.
Cleidocranial dysostosis (Table 1)
Autosomal dominant mutations in runt-related transcription factor 2
Defect in core-binding factor α-1, which is a transcription factor for osteocalcin
Affects intramembranous ossification: skull, clavicles, and pelvis
Evaluation
Delayed skull suture closure with frontal bossing present and delayed eruption of the
permanent teeth are observed.
Aplasia of the clavicles with ability to oppose the shoulders in front of the chest is observed.
Symphysis pubis is widened.
Coxa vara may be present.
Shortening of the middle phalanges of the third to fifth fingers

Cleidocranial dysostosis
Cleidocranial dysostosis is caused by dominant mutations in runt-related transcription
factor 2. This affects osteocalcin production by osteoblasts, leading to defects in
ossification. Patients may have absent or partial clavicles and defects in the pubic
symphysis.
Mucopolysaccharidoses disorders (Table 2)
Various genetic enzymatic defects result in intracellular accumulation of mucopolysaccharides
(Table 2)
All are autosomal recessive except type II Hunter syndrome, which is X-linked recessive.
MED (Table 1)

Autosomal dominant or autosomal recessive
Genes identified for this phenotype include cartilage oligomeric matrix protein and COL9A1,
COL9A2, and COL9A3, which encode a chain for type IX collagen (a linker protein for type II
collagen) and type X1 collagen.

MED
MED is caused by both autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive mutations.
Patients with the autosomal recessive form typically present with findings at birth, such
as clubfoot. Multiple genes are responsible for the dominant form; therefore, gene
panels that test multiple genes are helpful in diagnosing this disorder.
SED (Table 1)
Most common autosomal dominant form is SED congenita, which is apparent from birth and is
caused by mutations in COL2A1, which encodes type II collagen found in articular cartilage and
vitreous humor of the eyes. The proliferative zone of the growth plates is affected.
The uncommon X-linked recessive form is SED tarda, which is milder with later onset from
ages 8 to 10 years and is thought to involve the SEDL gene.

SED
Patients with SED may present with autosomal recessive and autosomal dominant
forms. Many different types exist, some more severe than others. Many different
causative genes have been identified, and diagnostic gene panels are useful in
determining a patient’s genetic profile.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Achondroplasia

Features include frontal bossing, button nose, trident hands (cannot approximate long and
ring fingers), thoracolumbar kyphosis (usually resolves with ambulation), lumbar stenosis with
lordosis and short pedicles, posterior radial head dislocation, champagne glass pelvic outlet,
and genu varum (Figure 4).
Foramen magnum stenosis and upper cervical stenosis may be present and cause central
apnea and weakness in the first few years of life.


Achondroplasia
Patients with achondroplasia typically present with frontal bossing, midface hypoplasia,
trident hands, lumbar lordosis, and genu varum. The main concern is foramen magnum
stenosis and upper cervical stenosis that may cause central apnea during the first 2
years of life. Patients need to be followed via repeated sleep studies to monitor for the
apnea and via developmental examinations to watch for signs of regression.
Pseudoachondroplasia (Table 1)
Cervical instability is common and must be assessed for (Figure 3).
Lower extremity bowing may be valgus, varus, or windswept.
Joints may be hyperlax in early life but later flexion contractures and early osteoarthritis.
Platyspondyly always is present; however, spinal stenosis is not present.

Pseudoachondroplasia
Psuedoachondroplasia may present as cervical instability. Although joints may have
hyperlaxity early in life, flexion contractures and early osteoarthritis are common later in
life. Platyspondyly always is present.
Diastrophic dysplasia (Table 1)
Cleft palate is present in 60% of patients.
Cauliflower ears are present in 80% of patients and develop after birth from cystic swellings in
the ear cartilage (Figure 1).
Hitchhiker thumbs are present (Figure 2).

Cervical kyphosis and thoracolumbar scoliosis often are present.
Joint contractures (hip flexion, genu valgum with dislocated patellae) and rigid clubfeet or skew
feet often are present.

Diastrophic dysplasia
Diastrophic dysplasia often presents as hitchhiker thumbs and cauliflower ears (no
trauma is necessary). Sixty percent of patients also have a cleft palate. Joint contractures
are common, and rigid clubfeet or skew feet often are present.
Mucopolysaccharidoses/Disorders (Table 2)
Evaluation
Diagnosis is by urine test to determine which mucopolysaccharide breakdown products and
glycosaminoglycans are present or by testing blood mucopolysaccharidoses panel enzyme
levels.
Note that enzymatic testing may be positive if urine testing is borderline or negative in
patients with mild symptoms who only present with bony abnormalities.
Molecular testing using genetic panels also is diagnostic.
Cervical instability is common and should be assessed for via flexion/extension lateral
cervical spine radiographs (Figure 3).

Mucopolysaccharidoses/Disorders
Mucopolysaccharidoses can be easily diagnosed via enzyme analysis. Urine and serum
testing are less sensitive but still useful for screening. Genetic testing panels also are
very helpful if suspicion is high. Cervical instability at C1-C2 is common; therefore,
flexion/extension cervical spine radiographs are indicated.
MED (Table 1)

Evaluation
Multiple abnormal epiphyses
Shortened metacarpals and metatarsals are present.
Valgus knees with a double layer patella are found.
May be mild to severe involvement of epiphyses; long-term prognosis ranges from mild joint
problems to end-stage osteoarthritis with severe joint contractures at a young age.
No spinal involvement should be present.

MED
MED is best diagnosed on skeletal survey if the growth plates are still open (skeletally
immature). Some patients may have a double-layered patella, which is a rare form of
bipartite patella that is pathognomonic for MED. Mild to severe involvement of the
epiphyses may be noted, with a reduction in epiphyseal size, flattening, and
fragmentation. Prognosis ranges from mild joint problems to severe osteoarthritis
requiring early joint arthroplasty of the large weight-bearing joints.
SED (Table 1) (Figure 5, A)
Evaluation
Cervical instability common in both forms.
SED congenita also has coxa vara, genu valgum, planovalgus feet, retinal detachment,
myopia, and hearing loss.
SED tarda does not result in lower extremity bowing but may result in dislocated hips.
Platyspondyly and delayed epiphyseal ossification as well as premature osteoarthritis are
associated with both types.

SED often results in cervical instability (C1-C2); therefore, this must be closely monitored.
Different types result in different presentations, with the severe SED congenita resulting
in many other symptoms, including retinal detachment, myopia, hearing loss, and other
orthopaedic conditions. Spine involvement includes platyspondyly and premature
osteoarthritis.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Techniques/Procedures
Achondroplasia
Nonsurgical management is typical for the thoracolumbar kyphosis that presents before
walking age. Avoidance of unsupported sitting may aid in prevention; a thoracolumbosacral
orthosis may be prescribed for some patients.
Genu varum is managed via growth modulation or osteotomies if progressive. More recent
literature supports the use of growth modulation for genu varum; however, it often requires
treatment at a young age to prevent severe deformity.1
Surgical Management
Techniques/Procedures
Surgical Approaches
Achondroplasia
Foramen magnum/upper cervical stenosis may require urgent decompression if spinal cord
compression is present.
In adult life, lumbar stenosis may require decompression and/or fusion.
Limb lengthening is controversial and does not manage the other dysmorphic features; if
lower limb lengthening is performed, humeral lengthening also is indicated.
Growth hormone is not effective at increasing stature.
Selective FGFR3 inhibitor drug therapies and CNP therapies (acting downstream of FGFR3)
currently are being investigated in clinical trials.

Diastrophic dysplasia (Table 1)
Surgical management for progressive spinal deformity or spinal cord compromise; cervical
kyphosis may resolve spontaneously but must be carefully monitored.
Surgical management is indicated for progressive, symptomatic lower extremity deformity;
recurrence of deformity is common.
The cauliflower ear deformity may be improved via early compressive bandaging (Figure 1).

Cleidocranial dysostosis (Table 1)
Progressive coxa vara is managed via intertrochanteric osteotomy.
The other features are managed supportively.
MED (Table 1)
For patients with bilateral Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, rule out MED.
Progressive genu valgum can be managed via hemiepiphysiodesis or osteotomy.
Painful, stiff joints are managed via physical therapy and NSAIDs; end-stage osteoarthritis is
managed via joint arthroplasty.
SED (Table 1)
Cervical instability is stabilized via posterior cervical fusion.
Progressive, symptomatic lower extremity deformity should be corrected via osteotomies,
being careful to assess the entire limb for deformities in joints above and below and
recognizing that early osteoarthritis and joint arthroplasty are likely (Figure 5, B).
Custom joint implants likely are necessary because of abnormal anatomy and the small size
of joints and bones; currently, these implants easier to order given the advent of digital
printing and newer technologies.
